anchors.paper_title: Task-Level Value Affects Trial-Level Reward Processing
anchors.reason: Dataset README cites this preprint; it reports the same three-task average-value study (RewP, gambling tasks) by the same authors.

metadata.methods_description: Twelve participants each completed three learning tasks (low-value, high-value, and mid-value) of 144 trials each. Each task required learning cue-response mappings for six cues, responding with the 'd' (left) or 'k' (right) key. Feedback validity was 0.5 for low-value cues and 0.8 for high-value cues. The mid-value task mixed three low-value and three high-value cues.

citation_details.title: Reward positivity affects temporal interval production in a continuous timing task
citation_details.author: Yan Yan, Laurence Tudor Hunt, Cameron Dale Hassall
citation_details.abstract: The neural circuits of reward processing and interval timing (including the perception and production of temporal intervals) are functionally intertwined, suggesting that it might be possible for momentary reward processing to influence subsequent timing behavior. Previous animal and human studies have mainly focused on the effect of reward on interval perception, whereas its impact on interval production is less clear. In this study, we examined whether feedback, as an example of performance-contingent reward, biases interval production. We recorded EEG from 20 participants while they engaged in a continuous drumming task with different realistic tempos (1728 trials per participant). Participants received color-coded feedback after each beat about whether they were correct (on time) or incorrect (early or late). citation_details.title: Neural substrates of the interaction between effort-expenditure reward decision-making and outcome anticipation
citation_details.author: Lingling Wang, Jiao Wang, Bing-hui Liu, Donghao Tuo, Simon S. Y. Lui, Weiqing Wan, Jia Huang, Raymond C. K. Chan
citation_details.abstract:
OBJECTIVE
Reward anticipation is important for future decision-making, possibly due to re-evaluation of prior decisions. However, the exact relationship between reward anticipation and prior effort-expenditure decision-making, and its neural substrates are unknown.


METHOD
Thirty-three healthy participants underwent fMRI scanning while performing the Effort-based Pleasure Experience Task (E-pet). Participants were required to make effort-expenditure decisions and anticipate the reward.


RESULTS
We found that stronger anticipatory activation at the posterior cingulate cortex was correlated with slower reaction time while making decisions with a high-probability of reward. citation_details.title: Unit Size Determination for Exploratory Brain Imaging Analysis: A Quest for a Resolution-Invariant Metric
citation_details.author: Jihnhee Yu, HyunAh Lee, Zohi Sternberg
citation_details.abstract: Defining an adequate unit size is often crucial in brain imaging analysis, where datasets are complex, high-dimensional, and computationally demanding. Unit size refers to the spatial resolution at which brain data is aggregated for analysis. Optimizing unit size in data aggregation requires balancing computational efficiency in handling large-scale data sets with the preservation of brain activity patterns, minimizing signal dilution. We propose using the Calinski–Harabasz index, demonstrating its invariance to sample size changes due to varying image resolutions when no distributional differences are present, while the index effectively identifies an appropriate unit size for detecting suspected regions in image comparisons. The resolution-independent metric can be used for unit size evaluation, ensuring adaptability across different imaging protocols and modalities. citation_details.title: LaBraM at Scale: Scaling Data and Models for EEG Pretraining
citation_details.author: Junyu Pan, Ruicheng Yin, Bao‐Liang Lu, Dongsheng Li, Wei-Long Zheng, Yansen Wang
citation_details.abstract: LaBraM, an early EEG foundation model, demonstrated that large-scale EEG pretraining can yield strong representations for diverse downstream tasks. Building on this foundation, we expand pretraining data and model capacity while retaining its core encoder and objective. We train ten encoders with 5.8 million to 1.97 billion parameters on three EEG collections spanning 25,067 to 79,910 hours, adapting signal preparation and training to heterogeneous recordings. Across 23 tasks, Atom-L* reaches 59.05% mean balanced accuracy at its best evaluated full fine-tuning (Full-FT) checkpoint, 3.61 percentage points above the strongest baseline EEG foundation model. Quark-G leads linear probing (LP) at 54.33%, a 1.24-point margin. Both also lead average task rank. At the last evaluated checkpoints, larger encoders improve Full-FT more consistently than LP, and stronger LP does not guarantee stronger Full-FT. citation_details.title: The Effects of Learnability and Reward Responsiveness on Reward Processing
citation_details.author: Abigail Oloriz, Olave E. Krigolson, Cameron Dale Hassall
citation_details.abstract: Abstract For methodological reasons, reward processing is commonly studied using random feedback and unlearnable tasks. It remains unclear whether task learnability influences reward-related brain activity, and whether this effect depends on individual differences such as reward responsiveness. We addressed this question by administering a behavioural activation system (BAS) scale before recording electroencephalography (EEG) while participants completed learnable and unlearnable versions of the “doors” task, a standard two-choice paradigm. Despite matched outcome likelihoods across conditions, participants reported greater motivation, enjoyment, and perceived performance in the learnable task.
